title: Quantum Machine Learning for Cybersecurity Applications: Simulation and Hardware Validation
authors: Zirui Zhu, Zisheng Chen, Xiangyang Li
abstract: Under tight feature and compute budgets, classical threat detection pipelines often degrade on near-decision-boundary events. Small quantum processors are now available, but existing work inadequately shows whether quantum components improve end-to-end threat detection under the above resource constrained conditions. This paper tries to address this gap with a hybrid architecture that uses a compact multilayer perceptron layer to compress the information in data and then routes the processed features to a few qubit quantum heads implemented in quantum support vector machine (QSVM) and variational quantum circuit (VQC) models. On a simulation platform, we benchmark these hybrid models against classical models with comparable parameter budgets on two representative cybersecurity tasks, network intrusion detection on NSL-KDD dataset and spam filtering on Ling-Spam dataset. To validate their precision on real quantum hardware, we deploy the best 4-qubit QSVM model on an IBM Quantum device with noise-aware execution, evaluated on a smaller sub-dataset. In the results, shallow quantum heads consistently match, and on difficult near-boundary cases modestly reduce missed attacks and false alarms compared to classical models using the same features. Hardware validation results track the simulation behavior closely enough that the remaining gap is dominated by device noise rather than model design. Furthermore, we conduct adversarial attacks to test the robustness of one QSVM model. Taken together, the study shows that even on small, noisy devices, carefully engineered quantum components may function as competitive, budget-aware components in practical cyber threat detection applications.
summary: This paper investigates using hybrid Quantum Machine Learning models, combining classical feature compression with quantum classifiers (QSVM/VQC), for cybersecurity tasks like intrusion and spam detection. The authors benchmark these models on simulation and validate them on real quantum hardware, showing that carefully engineered quantum components can provide competitive, budget-aware performance even on small, noisy devices.
main_problem: The paper addresses the gap in understanding how quantum components improve end-to-end threat detection in resource-constrained cybersecurity pipelines.
main_result: Shallow quantum heads, particularly the 4-qubit QSVM, modestly reduce missed attacks and false alarms on difficult near-boundary cases compared to classical models using the same features.
method: A hybrid architecture is employed, using a classical MLP for feature compression followed by quantum heads (QSVM or VQC) for classification, benchmarked against classical counterparts.
model_or_system: The system involves small quantum processors (NISQ era), validated on an IBM Quantum device. The models include QSVM using a fixed ZZFeatureMap and VQC using a trainable circuit structure.
key_observables: False Positive (FP) and False Negative (FN) shifts, macro-F1, AUROC, and AUPRC across intrusion and spam detection tasks.
important_parameters: Feature Budget ($q \in \{2, 4\}$), circuit depth, shot count, and adversarial perturbation strength ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The study assumes fixed preprocessing and MLP encoding to isolate the decision layer's contribution, and the remaining simulation-hardware gap is attributed to device noise.
figures_summary: Table IV shows robustness stress test results for the 4-qubit Ling-Spam MLP+QSVM, detailing performance drops under various adversarial attacks.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the hybrid architecture, benchmarks it on two datasets (NSL-KDD, Ling-Spam) comparing QSVM and VQC, validates the best model on real hardware, and concludes by testing the model's robustness against adversarial attacks.
why_interesting: While focused on cybersecurity, the work provides concrete, resource-aware benchmarks for applying quantum kernels (QSVM) and variational circuits (VQC) on near-term hardware, which is relevant for understanding noise-mitigated quantum computation.
